notes.title: Chapter map: Networking for AI systems
notes.html:
Stage:resolverouteconnectsecurebalanceframemessagecontractserverecoverper request

This section applies the whole pillar to AI traffic, and one idea runs through it: AI failures on the network are silent.

  • A buffered stream has the same status, bytes and total time.
  • A cut generation ends cleanly, with no error.
  • A hot prefix overloads one replica while the fleet average looks fine.
  • An SSRF through a tool looks like an ordinary fetch.

So every note ends in a measurement at the client or per replica, not a fleet-wide average.

Concept map

The four CORE notes form one argument: the path (168), the budget (169), the duration (170), the placement (172). The SUPPORTING notes apply it to voice, providers, tools, cost and tenants.

Green is CORE, blue is SUPPORTING; each blue node groups two notes. There are no BREADTH items, so there's no breadth.md. Neighbours: GPU and inference LB owns round robin vs least request; WebRTC vs WebSocket owns audio transport; the agentic pillar owns agent safety and cost.

172 is read fourth, before 171, because the CORE four build on each other; 175 right after 174 because 174 names the risk and 175 owns the control.

Users say the AI feels slow. Where do I look? Ask in this order. The first "yes" decides.

  • Two most-confused pairs: TTFB vs TTFT (first byte vs first token), and SSRF vs exfiltration (reaching in vs sending out).
  • Ten minutes before a tech discussion: say "five hops buffer"; say "setup + transit + gateway + queue + prefill"; say "heartbeat under half"; say "affinity with a cap"; say "retry only before the first token"; say "resolve, check, pin".

notes.title: Streaming LLM Tokens End to End — One Buffering Hop Undoes the Whole Stream
notes.html:
References

WHATWG HTML §9.2: Server-sent events · nginx: proxy_buffering and X-Accel-Buffering · Anthropic: Streaming messages · zlib manual: flush modes

TL;DR

A model streams tokens as Server-Sent Events, but users see them one by one only if every hop forwards bytes as they arrive. Five hops buffer by default:

  • The app writes into a framework buffer and doesn't flush.
  • Compression (gzip, brotli) waits for enough bytes to compress.
  • The reverse proxy (nginx proxy_buffering on) collects the response first.
  • A CDN or API gateway buffers or caches the response.
  • The client library reads the whole body before returning.

The trap: a buffered stream has the same status, the same bytes and the same total time. Only time to first token changes, from a few hundred milliseconds to the whole generation. TTFB stays low when the proxy streams headers early, so TTFB alone can't detect it.

Stage:resolverouteconnectsecurebalanceframemessagecontractserverecoverper request
Flow:model emits a tokenapp writes data: …\n\n and flushesno compression on text/event-streamproxy forwards with buffering offCDN passes throughclient reads line by linetoken on screen

Recall

Prompt Answer
Five hops that buffer? App, compression, reverse proxy, CDN or gateway, client library.
What does a buffered stream look like in metrics? Same status, bytes and total time; first token arrives at the end.
TTFB vs TTFT? First byte (often headers) vs first token; they diverge when a hop buffers.
One header that turns off nginx buffering per response? X-Accel-Buffering: no.
Why does gzip break streaming? It emits nothing until its buffer fills or it's flushed.
Draw by hand: five hops Five boxes left to right (app, gzip, proxy, CDN, client); under each, the setting that makes it stream.

The idea

A chat product works in development: tokens appear one by one. In production, users stare at a spinner for 8 seconds, then the whole answer appears at once. Status 200, same byte count, same total latency, no errors anywhere. Someone sets proxy_buffering off in nginx, and nothing changes: the load balancer in front added gzip, which holds every token until the stream ends. The stream was only as good as its worst hop.

The fix isn't one setting but a checklist, and the test for it is measuring first token at the client, through the full production path.

The trade: streaming makes a slow generation feel fast, and you pay with configuring every hop to forward bytes immediately, giving up compression and caching on that path, and testing it end to end, because one hop with default settings silently turns it back into a single late response.

How it works

The path, and what each hop needs.

Hop Default that bites Setting that streams
app framework buffers writes (WSGI, some ASGI middleware) yield per event; flush; no response-wide middleware that reads the body
compression gzip holds bytes until its block fills exclude text/event-stream, or flush each event (Z_SYNC_FLUSH)
nginx proxy_buffering on X-Accel-Buffering: no from the app, or proxy_buffering off on that location
CDN, API gateway buffer or cache whole responses; some cap response time a streaming-capable route, Cache-Control: no-cache
client response.json() or .text() waits for the end fetch body reader, EventSource, SDK stream()

Evolution

Lineage:2006 Opera ships SSE2009 SSE drafted in HTML52015 EventSource in every major browser except IE2020 Edge on Chromium closes the gap2023 LLM APIs standardise on SSE token streams2025 MCP Streamable HTTP streams tool results over SSE
  • Maturity: 🟢 Established (Nov 2026).
  • Changed recently: LLM APIs stream typed events (content deltas, tool-input deltas, thinking), not just text; gateways and CDNs added streaming modes for AI routes.
  • What won't change: any buffering hop turns a stream into one late response.

On the wire

Captured on localhost, 24 Nov 2026 (Python 3.15): a token server that waits 300 ms (queue and prefill), then sends 10 tokens 50 ms apart as SSE. A Python client recorded time to first byte and to first token, direct and through two proxies.

path                       TTFB      first token   tokens   last byte
direct                       5 ms        310 ms       10      853 ms
through streaming proxy      5 ms        310 ms       10      855 ms
through buffering proxy    847 ms        847 ms       10      847 ms   ← everything at once, at the end

Same 10 tokens, same 200 and the same total. Only first token moved, by the whole generation.

And gzip, compressing each token as an on-the-fly proxy would (zlib, gzip framing):

bytes emitted per token, no flush:     [10, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0]   + 50 at the end
bytes emitted per token, Z_SYNC_FLUSH: [28, 12, 11, 11, 11, 11, 11, 11, 11, 11]

The default that bites: nothing in the first output is a token (10 bytes is the gzip header). All tokens arrive when the stream closes.

Break it: the buffering proxy from the capture (Python 3.15, run 24 Nov 2026):

if mode == "buffer":
    body = b""
    while (c := up.recv(65536)): body += c     # wait for the upstream to finish
    conn.sendall(body)                           # then send it all
else:
    while (c := up.recv(65536)): conn.sendall(c) # forward each chunk as it arrives
# look for: TTFB and first token through each proxy
# naive belief predicts: buffering only adds a little latency, so tokens still trickle in

Run: through the buffering proxy, first byte and first token both arrived at 847 ms, the moment the generation finished, instead of 310 ms. The user waits for the entire answer either way.

Measure it

  • See it: curl -N through the production URL and watch tokens arrive; record first-token time at the client, not TTFB.
  • In production: client-side time to first token and inter-token gap p99 (RUM or SDK telemetry), compared with the model server's own first-token time; a gap equal to the generation length means a buffering hop.
  • Bounded by: SSE framing and replay → server-sent events; idle timeouts on long streams → long-lived connections.

Tech discussion

30-second answer: Token streaming works only if every hop forwards bytes immediately: the app flushes per event, compression is off for text/event-stream, the proxy's buffering is off (X-Accel-Buffering: no), the CDN or gateway passes it through, and the client reads incrementally. A buffered stream has the same status, bytes and total time, so I measure first token at the client through the real path, not TTFB at the server.

Q · Mechanism — Why can TTFB look fine while users see nothing? Some proxies send response headers as soon as the upstream does, then buffer the body. The client's first byte (headers) is quick, but the first token in the body waits for the buffer. TTFB measures the headers; TTFT measures the body. They diverge exactly when a hop buffers.

Q · Trade-off — Turn compression off for streams, or flush it per event? Off is simplest and safe: token streams are small and compress poorly per event anyway. Flushing per event (Z_SYNC_FLUSH) keeps compression but adds bytes per flush (11–12 per token in the capture, more than the token) and depends on every compressing hop flushing. Off for text/event-stream; flush only where bandwidth is genuinely scarce.

Q · Failure — Streaming works through the ALB but not through the CDN. Why? The CDN treats the response as cacheable or buffers it to apply its own compression or WAF inspection, and some cap total response time. Check whether the route has a streaming or no-buffering mode, send Cache-Control: no-cache, and make sure the CDN isn't adding compression on top of the origin's.

Q · Design — Ship token streaming so it stays working.

  • App: emit SSE events with X-Accel-Buffering: no and Cache-Control: no-cache, flush per event.
  • Config: compression excludes text/event-stream at every hop; proxies stream on AI routes.
  • Client: read the body incrementally; handle reconnect and partial events.
  • Test: a synthetic check through the public URL that fails if first token arrives later than half the total time.
  • Watch: client-side TTFT vs server-side TTFT.

Compare

SSE WebSocket Chunked JSON lines
Direction server to client both server to client
Works through ordinary HTTP proxies yes, if not buffered needs upgrade support yes, if not buffered
Reconnect and resume built into EventSource build it yourself build it yourself
Used by LLM APIs, MCP Streamable HTTP realtime voice, collaboration some internal APIs

Numbers

Number Value Context Source
First token through a buffering proxy 847 ms vs 310 ms 10-token stream measured on localhost, 24 Nov 2026
gzip output before flush 10 bytes (header only) 10 tokens compressed measured, zlib, 24 Nov 2026
Bytes per token with Z_SYNC_FLUSH 11–12 overhead of flushing measured, zlib, 24 Nov 2026
nginx proxy_buffering on the default that bites default (as of Nov 2026): nginx proxy module

Pitfalls

  • "proxy_buffering off fixes streaming"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: it's the first answer every search returns.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: it fixes one of five hops; compression, a CDN or the client can still hold every token until the end.
    ↳ Think instead: check all five hops, and measure first token at the client.
  • Don't measure streaming with TTFB.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: TTFB is the standard latency metric and is already on dashboards.
    ↳ What goes wrong: headers can arrive early while the body is buffered, so TTFB stays low while users see nothing.
    ↳ Do instead: measure time to the first data: event at the client.
  • Not the same: streamed vs fast
    ↳ Why they get mixed up: streaming makes a response feel fast, so teams report it as a latency win.
    ↳ Difference: streaming changes when the first token arrives, not the total; a buffered stream has the same total time.
    ↳ Think instead: TTFT is the streaming metric, total is the generation metric.
  • "Compression always helps"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: it saves bandwidth on every other response the service sends.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: without per-event flushes it emits nothing until the end; with them, it adds bytes per token.
    ↳ Think instead: exclude text/event-stream from compression.
  • Don't test streaming only against localhost or staging without the CDN.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: the dev path is quick to run and shows tokens arriving.
    ↳ What goes wrong: the hops that buffer (CDN, LB compression, WAF) exist only in production, so the test passes and users still wait.
    ↳ Do instead: a synthetic check through the public URL that fails when first token arrives late.
  • Shelf life: the five hops are durable; CDN streaming modes and SDK event types move.

Connections

Path:triage playbooksstreaming LLM tokenstime to first tokenlong-lived connections
  • Builds on server-sent events and HTTP/1.1 limits.
  • Owned elsewhere: streaming in agent products owns UX and event design.
  • Breaks when combined with compression, caching or WAF inspection on the streaming route.
  • Bounded by idle timeouts: a stream that pauses too long is cut, buffered or not.

notes.title: Time to First Token — Split It Into Five Before You Fix Any of It
notes.html:
References

Anthropic: Prompt caching · vLLM: Automatic prefix caching · RFC 8446 §2: TLS 1.3 handshake in one round trip · Cloudflare: The speed of light and the internet

TL;DR

Time to first token (TTFT) is the wait users feel. It's a sum of five terms, and only two are network:

TTFT = setup + transit + gateway + queue + prefill
       ─────────────── network     ──────────────── model side
setup    DNS + TCP + TLS on a new connection: 0 on a warm one
transit  one round trip for the request and the first byte back
gateway  auth, routing, rate limits, guardrails
queue    waiting for a batch slot on the model server
prefill  processing the prompt: grows with prompt tokens not already cached

On a warm connection, network is often under a fifth of TTFT. A long system prompt is a fixed prefill cost on every request, and prefix caching removes most of it. Split TTFT before optimising: the biggest term is usually not the one people guess.

Stage:resolverouteconnectsecurebalanceframemessagecontractserverecoverper request
Flow:client starts the requestsetup if the connection is newone round trip to the gatewaygateway checkswaits in the model's queueprefill over uncached prompt tokensfirst token streams back

Recall

Prompt Answer
TTFT's five terms? Setup, transit, gateway, queue, prefill.
Which two are network? Setup (DNS, TCP, TLS) and transit (one round trip).
Cheapest fix for a long system prompt? Prefix caching: keep the stable prefix first and identical.
Fibre latency rule of thumb? About 1 ms round trip per 100 km of path.
What does a warm connection remove? All of setup: no DNS, TCP or TLS round trips.
Draw by hand: the TTFT bar One horizontal bar split into five segments; shade setup and transit as network; mark which segment pooling, an edge and prefix caching each shrink.

The idea

A team's chat assistant has a 1.4 s TTFT, and the proposal is a CDN "to make it faster". Splitting it first:

  • setup 450 ms (a new connection every request, to a far region)
  • transit 150 ms
  • gateway 20 ms
  • queue 250 ms
  • prefill 540 ms (a 4,000-token system prompt plus tools, uncached)

The CDN, by terminating TLS nearby, would cut setup to 30 ms. Keeping connections warm cuts it to zero for free. Prefix caching cuts prefill by 500 ms. Together that's 460 ms, a third of the original, and none of it required a CDN.

The trade: measuring each term costs instrumentation at the client, the gateway and the model server, and it pays by pointing every optimisation at the term that is actually large, rather than at the network because the network is easiest to blame.

How it works

A model, Python 3.15, 24 Nov 2026, with illustrative inputs: round trip 150 ms to the inference region, 10 ms to a nearby edge, gateway 20 ms, queue 250 ms, prefill 8,000 tokens/s, a 4,000-token system prompt and a 300-token user turn.

Purple is network, red is model side.

Case TTFT Network share
cold connection, far region 1,408 ms 43 %
warm connection, far region 958 ms 16 %
edge terminates TLS, warm to the far region 987 ms 18 %
warm connection + prefix cache 458 ms 33 %
Term Lever Owner
setup pooled, kept-alive connections; TLS 1.3; resumption client and SDK config
transit inference capacity in the user's region placement, data path
gateway fewer synchronous checks; parallel guardrails platform team
queue capacity, admission control, load-aware routing inference LB
prefill prefix caching, shorter prompts, smaller model prompt and model owners

Evolution

Lineage:1997 HTTP/1.1 persistent connections remove per-request setup2018 TLS 1.3 cuts setup to one round trip2023 TTFT becomes the headline LLM latency metric; vLLM's paged attention2024 prompt caching in provider APIs and automatic prefix caching in vLLM2025 disaggregated prefill and decode pools
  • Maturity: 🟢 Established (Nov 2026).
  • Changed recently: provider APIs report cached input tokens per response; servers route by prefix to raise cache hits (inference LB).
  • What won't change: prefill grows with uncached prompt tokens, and distance sets a floor on transit.

On the wire

Captured on localhost, 24 Nov 2026 (the token server from item 168, 300 ms before its first token): first byte and first token are different events.

TTFB          5 ms    ← response headers: the server answered at once
first token 310 ms    ← queue + prefill happened after the headers

Reading the cache in a real API response, with the default that bites:

"usage": { "input_tokens": 312, "cache_read_input_tokens": 4012, "cache_creation_input_tokens": 0 }

cache_read_input_tokens > 0 means the prefix was reused. The default that bites: putting a timestamp or a request ID in the system prompt changes the prefix on every request, so the cache never hits and nothing warns you.

Break it: the TTFT model above (Python 3.15, 24 Nov 2026):

def ttft(setup_rtts, rtt, cached_sys):
    prefill = (USER + (0 if cached_sys else SYS)) / PREFILL_TPS
    return dict(setup=setup_rtts*rtt, transit=rtt, gateway=GW, queue=QUEUE, prefill=prefill)
# look for: which change takes the most off TTFT
# naive belief predicts: TTFT is mostly network, so an edge in front fixes it

Run: the edge took the cold case from 1,408 to 987 ms, but a warm connection alone got to 958 ms at no cost, and the prefix cache then took off another 500 ms. On a warm connection, network was 16 % of TTFT.

Measure it

  • See it: client timestamps for request start, first byte and first token; curl -w for setup terms (where latency goes).
  • In production: TTFT p50 and p99 at the client, the gateway and the model server; queue time and prefill time from the server; cache-read tokens as a share of input tokens.
  • Bounded by: streaming must work for TTFT to matter → streaming tokens; queue time → inference LB.

Tech discussion

30-second answer: TTFT is setup, transit, gateway, queue and prefill. Setup and transit are network; on a warm connection they're usually under a fifth. So I measure each term first. Warm pooled connections remove setup; inference in the user's region cuts transit; prefix caching cuts prefill for long stable prompts; queue time is a capacity and routing problem. An edge helps cold connections, but rarely more than pooling does.

Q · Mechanism — Why does prefix caching cut TTFT? Prefill computes attention keys and values for every prompt token before the first output token. If an identical prefix was processed recently on that server, its keys and values are reused, so only the new tokens are computed. A 4,000-token system prompt reused on every request goes from about 500 ms of prefill to nearly zero in the model above.

Q · Trade-off — Inference in every region or one central region? Every region cuts transit (about 1 ms per 100 km) and keeps data local, but spreads scarce GPU capacity thin, lowers cache hit rates per region and raises idle cost. Central is efficient and cache-friendly but adds 100–200 ms for distant users. Central with warm connections first; regional capacity when transit is a large share of TTFT for many users.

Q · Failure — TTFT p99 doubled with no traffic change. Where do you look? Split it. If queue time rose, a replica lost capacity or routing concentrated load. If prefill rose, the cache hit rate fell: a deploy changed the system prompt, or something per-request entered the prefix. If setup rose, connections stopped being reused. The term that moved names the owner.

Q · Design — Hit a 500 ms TTFT target.

  • Budget: allocate the 500 ms across the five terms and alert per term.
  • Setup: pooled HTTP/2 connections, kept warm across requests.
  • Prefill: stable prefix first (tools, system prompt), volatile content last; verify cache reads.
  • Queue: load-aware routing and admission control; shed before queueing.
  • Transit: capacity in the regions where most users are.

Compare

Lever Term it cuts Typical saving Cost
warm connections setup all of it pool configuration
edge TLS termination setup on cold connections most of it edge config, one more hop
regional inference transit 50–200 ms for distant users GPUs in more regions
prefix caching prefill most of the cached prefix prompt layout discipline
more capacity queue depends on load money

Numbers

Number Value Context Source
Model: cold, far region 1,408 ms 43 % network derived; model run 24 Nov 2026
Model: warm + prefix cache 458 ms from 958 ms warm derived; model run 24 Nov 2026
Fibre round trip ~1 ms per 100 km light at ~2/3 c, both directions derived from the speed of light in glass
TLS 1.3 full handshake 1 round trip before the request spec (as of Nov 2026): RFC 8446 §2

Pitfalls

  • "TTFT is a network problem"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: the word "latency" makes everyone look at the network first.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: on a warm connection, queue and prefill are usually most of it; in the model, network was 16 %.
    ↳ Think instead: split into five terms and fix the biggest.
  • Don't put per-request values in the prompt prefix.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: a timestamp or request ID in the system prompt feels harmless and helps debugging.
    ↳ What goes wrong: every request has a new prefix, so the cache never hits and prefill pays full price.
    ↳ Do instead: stable content first, volatile content after the cache breakpoint.
  • Not the same: TTFB vs TTFT
    ↳ Why they get mixed up: both measure "time until something comes back".
    ↳ Difference: TTFB is the first byte, often headers; TTFT is the first generated token, after queue and prefill.
    ↳ Think instead: measure the first token event, not the first byte.
  • "A CDN in front makes the model respond faster"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: CDNs speed up websites.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: it can cut setup on cold connections, but it can't cache generations, shorten queues or speed up prefill.
    ↳ Think instead: warm connections first; an edge only if cold setup is large.
  • Don't open a new connection per request from your backend to the provider.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: a fresh HTTP client per call is the simplest code to write.
    ↳ What goes wrong: every call pays DNS, TCP and TLS again: 450 ms per request in the model's far region.
    ↳ Do instead: one long-lived client per process, reused across calls.
  • Shelf life: the five-term split is durable; cache pricing, minimum prefix lengths and prefill speeds move.

Connections

Path:streaming tokenstime to first tokenlong-lived connections
  • Builds on where latency goes and pooling.
  • Owned elsewhere: context engineering owns prompt layout for caching; agent latency owns multi-call budgets.
  • Breaks when combined with a buffering hop: low TTFT at the server, high at the client.
  • Bounded by the speed of light: transit can only shrink by moving capacity.

notes.title: Long-Lived Connections at Scale — Idle Timers, Heartbeats and Drains for Multi-Minute Generations
notes.html:
References

AWS: ALB connection idle timeout · AWS: NAT gateway idle timeout (350 s) · Cloudflare: Error 524, a timeout occurred · WHATWG HTML §9.2: SSE comments as keep-alives

TL;DR

An AI response can stream for minutes and go silent for long stretches: reasoning, tool calls, a queue. Every hop on the path has an idle timer that cuts a connection with no bytes, usually at 60 s, and it does so silently:

  • The client gets no error, only a stream that ends early with no final event.
  • The server keeps generating, because a dropped flow sends nothing back until the server tries to write.

Three rules:

  • Heartbeat (an SSE comment : keep-alive) at under half the smallest idle timer on the path.
  • Raise the timers you own; you can't raise a carrier NAT's or a corporate proxy's.
  • Drain on deploy for as long as the longest generation, or make streams resumable.
Stage:resolverouteconnectsecurebalanceframemessagecontractserverecoverper connection
Flow:stream startsmodel thinks, no bytesheartbeat every 20 s keeps each hop's timer resettokens resumedeploy: old pod stops taking new streams, finishes current onesstream ends with a final event

Recall

Prompt Answer
What cuts a silent stream? Any hop's idle timer: LB, proxy, CDN, NAT, corporate proxy.
Heartbeat interval? Under half the smallest idle timer: 20–25 s behind a 60 s ALB.
How does the client know it was cut? Only by the missing final event ([DONE], message_stop).
Why does the server keep generating? No FIN or RST reaches it until it writes into the dead connection.
Does TCP keepalive help? Not for HTTP-layer idle timers, which count application bytes.
Draw by hand: the timer stack A horizontal path: client, corporate proxy, CDN 100 s, ALB 60 s, nginx 60 s, app; circle the smallest; draw heartbeat ticks at 20 s.

The idea

An agent answers a hard question: 10 seconds of tokens, then 90 seconds of reasoning and tool calls with nothing sent, then the rest. Users report answers that "just stop". There's no error in any log. The ALB's 60 s idle timer fired during the silence and closed both sides. The browser saw a normal end of stream. The model server learned nothing until it tried to write the next token, and by then it had spent 30 more seconds of GPU on an answer nobody would read.

A comment line every 20 seconds (: keep-alive, which SSE clients ignore) keeps every hop's timer from expiring. The user sees no difference, and the answers complete.

The trade: heartbeats and long timeouts keep slow generations alive through every hop, and you pay with a few bytes per stream every 20 seconds, connections held open for minutes (memory, file descriptors, LB capacity), and deploys that must wait for the longest stream or break it.

How it works

The smallest timer on the path decides; you control only some of them.

Hop Idle timer default You can raise it?
AWS ALB 60 s (up to 4,000 s) yes
nginx proxy_read_timeout 60 s between reads yes
Cloudflare proxied request 100 s to first byte, then 524 plan-dependent
AWS NAT gateway 350 s idle no
corporate proxy, carrier NAT unknown, often 30–120 s no
Problem Fix
silence cuts the stream SSE comment every 20 s; WebSocket ping frames
a cut looks like a normal end require a final event; treat its absence as an error and resume
GPU keeps working after a cut check the connection between tokens; cancel generation on write failure
deploys cut streams drain for the longest generation, then close with a "resume" event

Evolution

Lineage:1990s NAT idle timers break long TCP sessions2011 WebSocket ping and pong (RFC 6455)2015 SSE comments used as keep-alives2023 LLM streams expose 60 s defaults everywhere2025 reasoning models stream minutes of silence; providers send ping events
  • Maturity: 🟢 Established (Nov 2026).
  • Changed recently: provider APIs send periodic ping events during long streams; agent runs move to background jobs with resumable event streams.
  • What won't change: the smallest idle timer on the path decides, and you don't own all of them.

On the wire

Captured on localhost, 24 Nov 2026 (Python 3.15): a token server that sends one token, stays silent for 4 s, then sends three more; between it and the client, a proxy that closes after 2 s with no bytes.

quiet 4 s, proxy idle 2 s:             tokens 1   closed at 2,003 ms   [DONE] NO   ← cut, no error to the client
quiet 4 s + heartbeat 1 s, idle 2 s:   tokens 4   closed at 4,184 ms   [DONE] yes
server log, first case:  BrokenPipeError at ~4 s   ← it found out only when it wrote the next token

The heartbeat on the wire is one SSE comment line, which clients ignore:

data: {"type":"content_block_delta", ...}

: keep-alive

: keep-alive

data: {"type":"content_block_delta", ...}

The default that bites: the client's EventSource sees the cut as a normal close and reconnects, possibly starting a new, paid generation.

Break it: the idle proxy from the capture (Python 3.15, run 24 Nov 2026):

up.settimeout(idle)                       # 2.0 s with no bytes from upstream
try:
    while (c := up.recv(65536)): conn.sendall(c)
except (TimeoutError, socket.timeout):
    pass                                  # close both sides: no error sent, nothing logged
# look for: whether the client can tell a cut from a finished stream
# naive belief predicts: a timed-out stream shows up as an error somewhere

Run: the client got one token and a clean close at 2,003 ms, with no status change and no error. Only the missing [DONE] showed the answer was incomplete, and the server didn't notice for another 2 s.

Measure it

  • See it: stream through the production path with an artificial 90 s silence; check whether the final event arrives.
  • In production: share of streams that end without a final event, stream duration histogram with spikes at 60 s or 100 s, GPU-seconds spent after the client disconnected, open connections per instance.
  • Bounded by: WebSocket specifics → WebSocket operational reality; deploy mechanics → rollouts.

Tech discussion

30-second answer: AI streams go silent for minutes during reasoning and tool calls, and every hop has an idle timer, usually 60 s, that cuts silently. I send an SSE comment heartbeat at under half the smallest timer, raise the timers I own, require a final event so a cut is detectable, cancel generation when the client is gone, and drain deploys for the longest generation or make streams resumable.

Q · Mechanism — Why doesn't the model server notice the client left? An idle timer on a middle hop closes its two connections. The server's connection to that hop gets a FIN, but the server is busy computing and isn't reading or writing. It learns only when the next write fails, which can be seconds or minutes later. Checking for disconnect between tokens, and cancelling, saves that GPU time.

Q · Trade-off — Raise every timeout to an hour, or heartbeat? Long timeouts protect against silence on hops you own, but keep dead connections around for an hour, and don't help on hops you don't own. Heartbeats work across every hop, cost a few bytes, and keep timeouts short enough to clean up dead peers. Heartbeat always; raise owned timeouts moderately.

Q · Failure — Streams end at exactly 100 seconds for some users only. Why? A timer at 100 s on part of the path: Cloudflare's proxy timeout is 100 s, and those users go through the proxied hostname. Check which hostname and route they use, and whether the stream sends any bytes in the first 100 s; a long queue or reasoning phase before the first byte trips it.

Q · Design — Agent runs that last 20 minutes.

  • Don't hold one HTTP request for 20 minutes: start a background run, return a run ID.
  • Stream events from the run with IDs; the client reconnects with Last-Event-ID and replays missed events.
  • Heartbeat every 20 s on the event stream.
  • Deploys move runs, not connections: the run continues on a worker; only the viewing stream reconnects.

Compare

Keep-alive Layer Resets HTTP proxy idle timers Use for
SSE comment : keep-alive application yes SSE token streams
WebSocket ping frame WebSocket yes, through WebSocket-aware proxies realtime and voice
provider ping events application yes consuming provider streams
TCP keepalive TCP no NAT and firewall state only

Numbers

Number Value Context Source
ALB idle timeout 60 s default, up to 4,000 s per load balancer default (as of Nov 2026): AWS ALB docs
NAT gateway idle timeout 350 s not configurable default (as of Nov 2026): AWS NAT gateway docs
Cloudflare proxy timeout 100 s, then 524 proxied requests default (as of Nov 2026): Cloudflare 524 docs
Captured cut 2,003 ms, 1 of 4 tokens 2 s idle proxy measured on localhost, 24 Nov 2026

Pitfalls

  • "No errors in the logs means streams complete"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: every other failure in the system shows up as an error.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: an idle cut closes the connection cleanly; the client sees a normal end and no hop logs a failure.
    ↳ Think instead: count streams without a final event.
  • Don't set the heartbeat near the timeout.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: 55 s behind a 60 s timer looks efficient.
    ↳ What goes wrong: one delayed heartbeat (a GC pause, a slow write) and the timer fires first.
    ↳ Do instead: under half the smallest timer: 20–25 s for 60 s.
  • Not the same: TCP keepalive vs application heartbeat
    ↳ Why they get mixed up: both are "keepalives" that send periodic packets.
    ↳ Difference: TCP keepalive probes carry no application bytes, so HTTP proxies' idle timers ignore them; an SSE comment or WebSocket ping resets them.
    ↳ Think instead: heartbeat at the layer whose timer you need to reset.
  • "A disconnected client stops the generation"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: the request is gone, so the work should be too.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: the server finds out only when a write fails, and many frameworks don't cancel the model call even then.
    ↳ Think instead: check for disconnect between tokens and cancel explicitly.
  • Don't deploy with a drain shorter than the longest generation.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: the default 30 s grace period works for normal APIs.
    ↳ What goes wrong: every stream longer than the grace period is cut mid-answer, at every deploy.
    ↳ Do instead: drain for the longest stream, or make streams resumable and close with a resume event.
  • Shelf life: idle timers and heartbeat rules are durable; vendor defaults and provider event types move.

Connections

Path:time to first tokenlong-lived connectionsvoice agentsinference LB
  • Builds on the timeout hierarchy and WebSocket operational reality.
  • Owned elsewhere: long-horizon runs owns background runs and resumption.
  • Breaks when combined with reasoning or tool phases longer than the smallest timer and no heartbeat.
  • Bounded by hops you don't own: a corporate proxy's timer can only be beaten with heartbeats.

notes.title: Voice Agents — The Network's Share of Every Turn
notes.html:
References

ITU-T G.114: one-way delay guidance · LiveKit: Agents deployment and regions · OpenAI: Realtime API over WebRTC · Deepgram: streaming speech-to-text

TL;DR

A cascaded voice agent crosses the network five times on every turn between the user stopping and the bot starting to speak:

turn network time = ½ user RTT  +  STT RTT  +  model RTT  +  TTS RTT  +  ½ user RTT
                    audio in      final words  first token  first audio   audio out
                  + setup round trips on any connection that isn't warm

The provider hops run once per turn, so where they sit decides most of it. All in one region with warm connections, the network costs tens of milliseconds; providers on another continent cost half a second; cold connections per turn cost more than the whole budget. The transport choice for the audio itself belongs to WebRTC vs WebSocket.

Stage:resolverouteconnectsecurebalanceframemessagecontractserverecoverper request
Flow:user's audio to the nearest media edgeagent in that regionSTT, model, TTS in the same region on warm streaming connectionsaudio back to the user

Recall

Prompt Answer
How many network crossings per turn? Five: audio in, STT, model, TTS, audio out.
Which term grows fastest with bad placement? The three provider round trips: they repeat every turn.
What do cold connections add? Setup round trips (TCP, TLS) to each provider, on every turn.

The idea

A team picks the best STT, model and TTS vendors, each in a different region, and runs the agent where their other services live. Each choice is reasonable alone. Together, every turn pays three long round trips, and the HTTP client opens a new connection per call, adding setup each time. The bot answers 1.4 s after the user stops, of which the network is most. Moving the agent next to the media edge and choosing provider regions to match cut it to tens of milliseconds, without changing a single vendor.

The trade: co-locating the agent, media server and providers makes the network nearly free per turn, and you pay by choosing regions and sometimes vendors by distance, and by running agent capacity in every region where you have users.

How it works

Derived on 24 Nov 2026 from the formula above, with illustrative round trips: user to edge 40 ms, within a region 2 ms, across regions 150 ms.

Layout Network time per turn
agent, media and providers in the user's region, warm 46 ms
providers in another region, warm 490 ms
providers in another region, new connections to model and TTS each turn 1,390 ms
agent and providers together, far from the user (RTT 250 ms) 256 ms
Hop Design rule
user ↔ media edge nearest edge; WebRTC with TURN fallback (WebRTC for voice AI)
edge ↔ agent same region; the SFU dispatches the agent nearby
agent ↔ STT one streaming connection per call, opened at call start
agent ↔ model, TTS pooled, kept warm across turns; streaming responses
telephony SIP trunk in the agent's region

Evolution

Lineage:1990s VoIP and G.114's 150 ms guidance2011 WebRTC2023 cascaded voice agents (STT, LLM, TTS)2024 realtime speech-to-speech APIs collapse three provider hops into one2025 agent frameworks dispatch workers next to the SFU
  • Maturity: 🟢 Established (Nov 2026).
  • Changed recently: speech-to-speech models remove two provider hops per turn; providers offer regional endpoints for STT and TTS.
  • What won't change: every hop on the turn costs at least one round trip.

On the wire

What a warm provider connection looks like from the agent, with the default that bites:

client = httpx.AsyncClient(http2=True, timeout=httpx.Timeout(10.0, connect=2.0))  # one per process
# per turn: await client.post(TTS_URL, json=…)   ← reuses the open connection: 1 RTT, no setup
# the default that bites: `async with httpx.AsyncClient() as c:` inside the turn handler
# opens and closes a connection per turn, adding TCP + TLS round trips every time

Measure it

  • See it: per-turn timestamps at the agent for audio received, final transcript, first token, first TTS byte and first audio sent.
  • In production: per-provider round trip and connection reuse rate; end-of-speech to first-audio p50 and p95 by user region; share of turns paying connection setup.
  • Bounded by: the full turn budget → the latency budget; audio transport → WebRTC vs WebSocket.

Tech discussion

30-second answer: A cascaded voice turn crosses the network five times: audio in, STT, model, TTS, audio out. The three provider hops repeat every turn, so I put the agent next to the user's media edge and pick provider regions to match, with warm streaming connections opened at call start. That's tens of milliseconds; the same vendors across regions cost about half a second, and cold connections per turn more than a second.

Q · Mechanism — Why does a new connection per turn hurt so much? Each new connection pays TCP and TLS round trips before the request, about three round trips with DNS. Across regions at 150 ms, that's 450 ms per provider per turn. A connection opened at call start and reused pays it once per call instead.

Q · Trade-off — Best-in-class vendor far away, or a good one nearby? Each 150 ms round trip repeated every turn is a large share of an 800 ms budget, and no model quality hides a slow reply in conversation. Prefer a nearby region of the same vendor; if the best vendor has no nearby region, measure whether its quality gain is worth the per-turn delay.

Numbers

Number Value Context Source
Per-turn network, co-located and warm 46 ms illustrative RTTs derived, 24 Nov 2026
Per-turn network, providers across regions, cold 1,390 ms illustrative RTTs derived, 24 Nov 2026
One-way delay for natural conversation under 150 ms mouth to ear spec (as of Nov 2026): ITU-T G.114

Pitfalls

  • "Network latency is fixed; only the models matter"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: the model's time to first token is the biggest single number on the dashboard.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: three provider round trips per turn, set by placement, can add half a second or more.
    ↳ Think instead: sum the five crossings and place for them.
  • Don't create an HTTP client inside the turn handler.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: async with httpx.AsyncClient() is the idiomatic, tidy pattern.
    ↳ What goes wrong: every turn opens a new connection to each provider and pays setup round trips.
    ↳ Do instead: one client per process, or connections opened at call start.
  • Not the same: the agent's region vs the user's region
    ↳ Why they get mixed up: teams deploy where their other services already run.
    ↳ Difference: the agent must be near the user's media edge and its providers; your database region matters less.
    ↳ Think instead: place agents per user region.
  • Don't benchmark from the office next to the servers.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: it's the fastest place to try the bot during development.
    ↳ What goes wrong: a 2 ms user RTT hides the half of the turn real users pay over mobile networks and distance.
    ↳ Do instead: test from user regions over phone networks, and track latency by region.
  • Shelf life: the five-crossing sum is durable; provider regions and speech-to-speech APIs move.

Connections

Path:long-lived connectionsvoice agentsinference LB
  • Builds on WebRTC for voice AI and time to first token.
  • Owned elsewhere: WebRTC vs WebSocket owns audio transport; the voice pillar owns the turn (budget, latency playbook).
  • Breaks when combined with providers chosen without regard to region.
  • Bounded by distance: a far user pays the audio crossings whatever the backend does.

notes.title: Inference Load Balancing — Cache Affinity Against Load, and the Hot Prefix
notes.html:
References

Mirrokni, Thorup, Zadimoghaddam: Consistent hashing with bounded loads (2018) · vLLM: Automatic prefix caching · Gateway API Inference Extension: endpoint picker · SGLang: RadixAttention and cache-aware routing

TL;DR

Model servers cache the attention state (KV cache) of prompts they've seen. A request whose prefix (system prompt, tools, earlier turns) is already cached on a replica skips most of its prefill. That makes where a request goes change how much work it is. Two goals pull apart:

  • Load: send to the least busy replica (item 146 owns least request vs round robin).
  • Affinity: send to the replica that already caches this prefix.

Pure affinity hashes a hot prefix (a popular system prompt) onto one replica and overloads it. Pure load-balancing scatters prefixes and wastes the cache. Production converges on affinity with a load cap: go to the prefix's home replica unless it's above a bound, then to the least-loaded replica that also holds the prefix.

Stage:resolverouteconnectsecurebalanceframemessagecontractserverecoverper request
Flow:request arriveshash its prefix to a home replicahome under the load cap? send there, cache hitover the cap? least-loaded replica that caches the prefixnone? least-loaded replica, which then caches it too

Recall

Prompt Answer
Why does routing change the work? A cached prefix skips most of its prefill.
What goes wrong with pure prefix hashing? A hot prefix lands on one replica and overloads it.
What goes wrong with pure least-load? Prefixes scatter, hit rates fall, every replica does more prefill.
The compromise? Consistent hashing with bounded loads: home replica unless over a cap.
What signal beats the proxy's own in-flight count? The server's queue depth and KV-cache use, reported by the server.
Draw by hand: bounded-load routing A ring of 8 replicas; a request's prefix hashes to one; a dashed cap line on each replica's load bar; an arrow spilling to the next least-loaded holder when the bar crosses the line.

The idea

A platform serves one assistant whose 4,000-token system prompt appears on 30 % of requests. The team switches from least request to prefix hashing to raise cache hits, and the hit rate jumps from 33 % to 86 %. Within minutes one replica's queue grows without bound: every request with that popular prompt hashes to it, and its share of traffic exceeds what one replica can serve. Rolling back restores the latency and loses the cache gains.

Bounding the load fixes both. The popular prefix still goes to its home replica while that replica has room, and spills to a second and third replica when it doesn't. Those replicas then cache it too, so the spill is still mostly cache hits.

The trade: cache-aware routing cuts prefill work and TTFT for repeated prefixes, and you pay with a router that needs the prefix (parsing the request), per-replica load signals that are fresh enough to trust, and a cap to tune, because affinity without one turns popularity into overload.

How it works

The routing decision.

A model, Python 3.15, 24 Nov 2026: 8 replicas, FIFO each, 12 requests/s; prefill 0.40 s on a miss and 0.05 s on a hit, decode 0.30 s; each replica caches its 6 most recent prefixes; 60 prefixes, one of them on 30 % of requests. The cap is 1.25 × the average in-flight count + 1.

Policy Cache hit rate TTFT p50 TTFT p99 Utilisation
least request 32.5 % 0.40 s 1.79 s ~88 %
prefix hash 85.7 % 0.59 s 1,673 s (the hot replica's queue never drains) hot replica > 100 %
hash + load cap 74.9 % 0.40 s 1.56 s ~66 %

The cap kept most of the cache gain and none of the overload. Higher hit rates also cut total work: the same traffic needed about a quarter less GPU time than with least request.

Evolution

Lineage:1997 consistent hashing (Karger et al.)2016 consistent hashing with bounded loads, adopted in HAProxy 1.7 and by Vimeo2023 vLLM paged KV cache2024 SGLang RadixAttention and cache-aware routing; automatic prefix caching in vLLM2025 Gateway API Inference Extension endpoint picker scores prefix match with queue depth; llm-d and disaggregated prefill/decode
  • Maturity: 🟡 Maturing (Nov 2026): cache-aware routing is in production at large providers, and the open-source pickers and scoring plugins change monthly.
  • Changed recently: routers score replicas on prefix match, queue depth and KV-cache use together; prefill and decode run on separate pools, so routing is two decisions.
  • What won't change: affinity and load pull apart, and every affinity scheme needs a bound.

On the wire

A bounded-load option in HAProxy, and the signals a picker reads from a vLLM server, with the default that bites:

backend chat
    balance hash req.hdr(X-Prefix-Key)       # affinity on a prefix key the gateway computed
    hash-balance-factor 125                  # bounded load: no server above 125 % of the average
# the default that bites: without hash-balance-factor, one hot key sends all its traffic to one server

# vLLM /metrics, read by an endpoint picker
vllm:num_requests_waiting{model_name="chat"} 3
vllm:gpu_cache_usage_perc{model_name="chat"} 0.82

Break it: the core of the routing model (Python 3.15, run 24 Nov 2026):

if policy == "prefix hash":
    r = h(p)                                           # always the home replica
else:                                                   # hash + load cap
    r = h(p); cap = 1.25 * (sum(inflight) + 1) / R + 1
    if inflight[r] > cap:
        holders = [i for i in range(R) if p in caches[i] and inflight[i] <= cap]
        r = min(holders or range(R), key=lambda i: inflight[i])
# look for: TTFT p99 under prefix hash
# naive belief predicts: a higher cache hit rate always means lower latency

Run: prefix hash had the highest hit rate (85.7 %) and by far the worst latency (p99 1,673 s), because the 30 % hot prefix needed more than one replica's capacity. Hit rate and latency moved in opposite directions until the cap was added.

Measure it

  • See it: per-replica in-flight requests and queue depth side by side with cache hit rate per replica, under a load test with a realistic (skewed) prefix mix.
  • In production: max-to-median queue depth across replicas, prefix cache hit rate (cached input tokens ÷ input tokens), TTFT p99, share of requests spilled by the cap, and the most popular prefixes' share of traffic.
  • Bounded by: Kubernetes mechanics → GPU and inference LB; what TTFT is made of → time to first token.

Tech discussion

30-second answer: With prefix caching, routing changes the work: a request sent to a replica that caches its prefix skips most of its prefill. Pure affinity overloads the replica that owns a hot prefix; pure least-load scatters prefixes and wastes the cache. I use affinity with a load cap: home replica unless it's over a bound, then the least-loaded replica that also holds the prefix. In the model, that kept a 75 % hit rate and the best p99.

Q · Mechanism — Why does the spill stay mostly cache hits? When the home replica is over the cap, the router prefers another replica that already holds the prefix. The first spill is a miss, but that replica now caches the prefix, so later spills hit. A hot prefix ends up cached on just enough replicas to carry its load, which is exactly the replication you want.

Q · Trade-off — Route in the gateway on a hash, or in a picker on live server metrics? A hash in the gateway is cheap, stateless and needs no server metrics, but it doesn't know real queue depth or memory. A picker that scrapes queue depth and KV-cache use makes better decisions but is a dependency with its own latency and staleness. Hash with a cap to start; a metric-driven picker when replicas differ (adapters, sizes) or load is very uneven.

Q · Failure — After a deploy, TTFT doubled for an hour, then recovered. Why? New replicas start with empty caches, and if the hash ring changed, many prefixes now map to replicas that don't hold them. Hit rate falls, prefill rises, and queues grow until caches refill. Roll out gradually, keep the ring stable (consistent hashing moves only a fraction of keys), and pre-warm replicas with the most popular prefixes.

Q · Design — Route a multi-tenant chat platform.

  • Key: a hash of the stable prefix (tenant system prompt, tools); multi-turn chats include the conversation, so follow-up turns go home.
  • Cap: bounded load at ~1.25 × average, spilling to replicas that hold the prefix.
  • Signals: queue depth and KV-cache use from each server, refreshed every second or faster.
  • Pools: separate pools for very long prompts so they don't evict everyone's cache (multi-tenant isolation).
  • Watch: hit rate and max-to-median queue depth together.

Compare

Policy Cache use Hot prefix Needs
round robin random spread nothing
least request / P2C random spread in-flight counts
prefix hash high one replica overloaded prefix key
hash with bounded load high spread over just enough replicas prefix key, load counts
endpoint picker (scored) high spread by live signals server metrics, a picker service

Numbers

Number Value Context Source
Model: hit rate, least request vs hash + cap 32.5 % vs 74.9 % 8 replicas, 30 % hot prefix derived; model run 24 Nov 2026
Model: TTFT p99, prefix hash 1,673 s (unbounded queue) hot replica over capacity derived; model run 24 Nov 2026
HAProxy hash-balance-factor 0 (off) by default 125 = 125 % of average default (as of Nov 2026): HAProxy docs
Keys moved when one of n servers changes about 1/n consistent hashing spec (as of Nov 2026): Karger et al. 1997

Pitfalls

  • "Maximise the cache hit rate"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: hits skip prefill, so more hits sounds strictly better.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: pure affinity got 86 % hits and an unbounded queue, because one replica took the whole hot prefix.
    ↳ Think instead: hit rate under a load cap, judged with p99.
  • Don't route on the proxy's in-flight count alone.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: every proxy has it, with no extra integration.
    ↳ What goes wrong: in-flight counts ignore cache state and prompt length, so the "least loaded" replica may be the slowest for this request.
    ↳ Do instead: add the server's queue depth, cache use and prefix match where you can.
  • Not the same: session affinity vs prefix affinity
    ↳ Why they get mixed up: both send related requests to the same replica.
    ↳ Difference: session affinity pins a user; prefix affinity groups everyone who shares a prompt, which is where most cache reuse is.
    ↳ Think instead: key on the shared prefix, not the user.
  • "A deploy doesn't change latency if capacity is the same"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: same number of replicas, same model.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: new replicas have empty caches and a changed ring remaps prefixes, so hit rates fall until caches refill.
    ↳ Think instead: roll gradually and pre-warm the popular prefixes.
  • Don't let very long prompts share a pool with chat traffic.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: one pool is simpler and uses GPUs fully.
    ↳ What goes wrong: long-context requests fill KV-cache memory and evict everyone's prefixes, so chat hit rates collapse.
    ↳ Do instead: a separate pool, or a cap on cache share, for long prompts.
  • Shelf life: bounded-load affinity is durable; picker plugins, metric names and prefill/decode splits move.

Connections

Path:voice agentsinference load balancingprovider timeouts and retries
  • Builds on GPU and inference LB and load balancing algorithms.
  • Owned elsewhere: item 146 owns round robin vs least request and InferencePool; item 169 owns what prefill costs.
  • Breaks when combined with a hot prefix and no load cap.
  • Bounded by signal freshness: routing on stale queue depths sends bursts to the same replica.

notes.title: Timeouts & Retries Against LLM Providers — A Gap Timer, Not a Total, and Retry Only Before the First Token
notes.html:
References

Anthropic: Errors (429, 529) and retries · Anthropic Python SDK: retries and timeouts · OpenAI Python SDK: retries and timeouts · HTTPX: timeouts (connect, read, write, pool)

TL;DR

An LLM call is a slow, streaming, rate-limited dependency. Three rules for the client:

  • Time it in two parts: a short limit to first token (catches queueing and stuck requests) and an inter-token gap limit (catches stalls). A single total timeout either kills long answers or takes minutes to notice a dead stream.
  • Retry only before the first token. After tokens have streamed, a retry starts a new, billed generation and the user sees the answer restart.
  • Retry the right errors, at the right pace: 429 and 529 (overloaded) and 5xx and connection errors, honouring retry-after, with a budget across all calls.

The SDKs' "10-minute timeout" is a per-read timer (httpx read=600), so it already behaves as a gap timer, and a 10-minute silence is how long a dead stream takes to notice.

Stage:resolverouteconnectsecurebalanceframemessagecontractserverecoverper request
Flow:connect (≤ 5 s)first token within the TTFT limit, or retry with jitterstream; each gap under the gap limitstall after tokens arrived: surface the error, don't silently regenerate429 or 529: wait retry-after, or fail over

Recall

Prompt Answer
The SDK's default timeout, really? connect 5 s; read, write, pool 600 s each: a per-read gap timer, not a total.
When is a retry safe? Before the first token; after it, a retry is a new, billed generation.
What does 529 mean at Anthropic? overloaded_error: the API is temporarily overloaded; retry with backoff or fall back.

The idea

A support assistant sets timeout=30 to "fail fast". Long answers still work, because the timer resets on every read. But a request queued 35 s before its first token fails, is retried twice by the SDK, and the user waits 90 s for an error.

Split timers fix it: 10 s to first token, then 20 s between tokens. Queued requests are retried quickly, stalls are caught in 20 s, and long answers complete.

The trade: explicit first-token and gap timers plus retry rules make failures fast and cheap, and you pay with writing that logic around the SDK (which offers one timer per read), and with deciding what the user sees when a stream breaks after it started.

How it works

Read from the installed packages on 24 Nov 2026 (uv run --with anthropic --with openai):

SDK Version Default timeout Retries Backoff
anthropic (Python) 2.13.0 connect 5 s; read, write, pool 600 s 2 0.5 s growing to 8 s, with jitter
openai (Python) 3.58.0 connect 5 s; read, write, pool 600 s 2 exponential, with jitter

Retried by default: 408, 409, 429, 5xx (including Anthropic's 529) and connection errors, unless the response says x-should-retry: false; retry-after is honoured. A timeout is retried too, so one call can take timeout × 3 in the worst case.

Error Means Do
429 rate_limit_error your limit (requests, tokens) wait retry-after; smooth your rate
529 overloaded_error provider-wide overload backoff; fall back to another model or region
5xx provider fault one retry with jitter, then fall back
stall after tokens stream broke mid-answer show what arrived, offer "continue", don't silently regenerate
400, 401, 404 your request is wrong never retry

Evolution

Lineage:2015 AWS publishes backoff with jitter2020 OpenAI SDK retries2023 Anthropic SDK with x-should-retry2024 529 overloads routine at peaks2025 AI gateways chain fallbacks across providers
  • Maturity: 🟢 Established (Nov 2026).
  • Changed recently: providers send retry-after on 429 and 529 and periodic ping events on long streams; AI gateways fail over between models and providers.
  • What won't change: a retry after the first token is a new generation.

On the wire

Captured on localhost, 24 Nov 2026: httpx 0.28.1 (the client both SDKs use) against the token server from item 170, with only a read timeout set:

/gen   read timeout 0.2 s → ReadTimeout after 0.26 s   ← first token at 0.3 s: the read timer acts as a TTFT timer
/think read timeout 2.0 s → ReadTimeout after 2.01 s   ← a 4 s silence mid-stream: acts as a gap timer
/think read timeout 4.5 s → ok, 4 tokens in 4.19 s
/think-hb read timeout 2.0 s → ok, 4 tokens in 4.18 s  ← total 4.2 s under a "2 s timeout": heartbeats reset it

The default that bites: timeout=30 reads as "30 seconds total", but it is 30 s per read, so it neither caps the total nor separates first token from gaps.

Measure it

  • See it: log time to first token, the largest inter-token gap, retries and their cause per call.
  • In production: 429 and 529 rates by model and region, retries per successful call (a retry budget), streams broken after first token, fallback share and its quality.
  • Bounded by: retry discipline → retries done right; idle timers on your own hops → long-lived connections.

Tech discussion

30-second answer: I time LLM calls in two parts: a short first-token limit and an inter-token gap limit, because a total timeout either kills long answers or detects stalls late; the SDK default is actually a 600 s per-read timer. I retry only before the first token, on 429, 529, 5xx and connection errors, honouring retry-after and within a budget, and fall back to another model when the provider is overloaded.

Q · Mechanism — Why is a retry after the first token different? The provider has started, and billed, a generation. A retry starts another from scratch with different sampling: the text restarts and changes, and you pay twice. Before the first token nothing was shown, so a retry is invisible and cheap.

Q · Trade-off — On 529, wait or fail over to another model? Waiting keeps quality consistent and is right for background work. Failing over keeps interactive latency but changes answers (different model, different behaviour) and needs a second integration kept tested. Background: honour retry-after. Interactive: one quick retry, then a tested fallback that already gets a small share of normal traffic.

Numbers

Number Value Context Source
SDK default timeouts connect 5 s; read, write, pool 600 s anthropic 2.13.0, openai 3.58.0 default (as of Nov 2026): read from the installed packages
SDK default retries 2 both SDKs default (as of Nov 2026): read from the installed packages
Anthropic backoff range 0.5–8 s with jitter default (as of Nov 2026): anthropic 2.13.0 constants
Worst-case wall time of one call timeout × 3 a timeout is retried derived from the defaults

Pitfalls

  • "timeout=30 caps the call at 30 seconds"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: that's what a timeout parameter means everywhere else.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: it's a per-read timer; a stream can run far longer, and with retries a failing call can take three times as long.
    ↳ Think instead: explicit first-token and gap timers, plus a deadline you enforce yourself.
  • Don't retry a stream that already produced tokens.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: the SDK or a wrapper retries automatically and the code looks the same.
    ↳ What goes wrong: the user sees the answer restart with different text, and you pay for two generations.
    ↳ Do instead: keep what arrived, report the break, offer to continue.
  • Not the same: 429 vs 529
    ↳ Why they get mixed up: both say "slow down" and both are retryable.
    ↳ Difference: 429 is your own rate limit, fixed by smoothing your traffic; 529 is the provider's overload, where fallback helps and smoothing doesn't.
    ↳ Think instead: 429 → pace yourself; 529 → back off or fail over.
  • "Our layer and the SDK can both retry"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: more retries feels more resilient.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: two retries in the SDK times three in your wrapper is nine calls per request during an overload, which deepens it.
    ↳ Think instead: one retrying layer; set max_retries=0 where your own policy retries.
  • Shelf life: the two-timer and before-first-token rules are durable; SDK defaults and error codes move.

Connections
